research_topics: scaled behavioral methods (think-aloud) for cognitive science
current_direction: Using LLMs as stimulus-computable cognitive models of human thought
Mechanistic accounts of in-context learning and belief dynamics in LLMs
Scaling classic cognitive-science methods (think-aloud) with language models
Language-mediated social learning, iterated learning and cultural transmission
LLM reasoning applied to formal math / interactive theorem proving
current_direction_basis: Inferred from the 2025-2026 works verified via OpenAlex in this task, not from the biography on the (stale) personal page. Specifically: Frank & Goodman, 'Cognitive Modeling Using Artificial Intelligence' (Annual Review of Psychology, 2025-09-12) drove the 'LLMs as stimulus-computable cognitive models' phrase -- its abstract states current models 'are stimulus computable, meaning that they can operate over stimuli that are similar to those experienced by people'. Bigelow, Wurgaft, ... Goodman et al., 'Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering' (arXiv 2511.00617, 2025-11-01) drove the in-context-learning/belief-dynamics phrase, and matches current PhD student Daniel Wurgaft's stated interest on the lab People page. Wurgaft, Prystawski, Gandhi, ... Goodman, 'Scaling up the think-aloud method' (arXiv 2505.23931, 2025-05-29) drove the scaled-methods phrase. Prystawski, Arumugam & Goodman, 'Lossy communication constrains iterated learning' (arXiv 2511.18220, 2025-11-22) plus Colas et al. 'Language and Experience' (arXiv 2509.00074, 2025-08-26) and the 2026 Psychological Review paper 'Learning from generic language' drove the social-learning / iterated-learning phrase. Xin et al., 'Automated Discovery of Tactic Libraries for Interactive Theorem Proving' (PACMPL, 2025-10-09) drove the formal-math phrase, corroborated by the lab publications page entry 'A survey on large language model reasoning failures' (2nd AI for Math Workshop @ ICML 2025).

evidence.title: Learning from generic language
evidence.summary: Journal article with Michael Henry Tessler in Psychological Review, publication date 2026-08-27 per OpenAlex. Most recent peer-reviewed item found; continues the lab's long-running work on how generic statements convey generalizable knowledge.

evidence.title: Lossy communication constrains iterated learning
evidence.summary: arXiv preprint (2025-11-22) by Ben Prystawski, Dilip Arumugam and Noah D. Goodman. Abstract asks whether large differences in ability between humans and other animals must be posited to explain human iterated learning. Prystawski is listed as a current CoCoLab graduate student.

evidence.title: Belief Dynamics Reveal the Dual Nature of In-Context Learning and Activation Steering
evidence.summary: arXiv preprint (2025-11-01) with Eric Bigelow, Daniel Wurgaft, YingQiao Wang, Tomer Ullman, Hidenori Tanaka and Ekdeep Singh Lubana. Interpretability-flavoured work on in-context learning; Wurgaft is a current CoCoLab graduate student whose People-page blurb names in-context learning and training dynamics.

evidence.title: Cognitive Modeling Using Artificial Intelligence
evidence.summary: Review article with Michael C. Frank in Annual Review of Psychology (2025-09-12). Abstract: 'Recent progress in artificial intelligence (AI) is exciting, but can AI models tell us about the human mind? ... one key difference in the current generation of models is that they are stimulus computable.' Signals the programmatic framing of the lab's current agenda.

evidence.title: Scaling up the think-aloud method
evidence.summary: arXiv preprint (2025-05-29) with Daniel Wurgaft, Ben Prystawski, Kanishk Gandhi, Cedegao E. Zhang and Joshua B. Tenenbaum. Three current CoCoLab graduate students are co-authors. Behavioural-data-collection work of the kind undergraduate RAs are often involved in.

state_rationale: ADVERSARIAL RE-VERIFICATION 2026-08-31: OPENING is UPHELD. https://cocolab.stanford.edu/join was re-fetched live in this task (HTTP 200) and carries a present-tense statement addressed to undergraduates specifically, verbatim: "Potential research assistants (Stanford undergraduate or masters): Please send the PI or this mailing list (cocomentorship@lists.stanford.edu) an email with a current CV (including relevant research and programming experience), describe why you want to join the lab and what type of projects you are interested in. Please also indicate whether you are looking for a paid or a volunteer / course credit position." This is not a PhD-applicant-only page: the graduate paragraph ('Potential graduate students: We are accepting strong applicants in Computer Science or Psychology. Please apply through your respective department...') is a separate paragraph, and the page explicitly CLOSES two other categories in its own words -- 'Potential research assistants (non-Stanford): We are generally unable to accommodate research assistants from outside Stanford' and 'High-school interns: We are unable to take high-school students at this time' -- while leaving the Stanford-undergraduate route open with a stated application procedure. Nothing on the page says the PI is not taking students. The URL resolves directly (no Google Doc, no form, no access wall). HONEST LIMITS, which is why confidence is 0.85 and not higher: (1) the page is undated -- there is no posting date, no deadline, no headcount, and the server returns no Last-Modified header, so the recency of the statement cannot be independently established, only that it is served today; (2) the lab People page, re-fetched in this task, has no undergraduate/RA section at all, so no current undergraduate is observable in the lab; (3) the page never states that funded/paid slots exist -- it only asks the applicant to say which they want, so the 'paid' signal was downgraded from 'verified' to 'likely'. Treat this as a standing, always-open application route with a real named intake channel, NOT as a posted funded vacancy for a specific quarter. Corroborating (not itself an opening): Stanford Profiles lists 'Supervised Undergraduate Research CS 195', 'Senior Project CS 191' and 'Special Laboratory Projects PSYCH 195' among his 2025-26 supervision listings, and the lab is demonstrably active (2026 Psychological Review article plus multiple 2025 preprints with current lab students). The stated ask is verbatim 'a current CV (including relevant research and programming experience)' plus a statement of why you want to join and what projects interest you; the page words nothing as REQUIRED versus PREFERRED, so no such split is recorded.
